headline: The Cut Off Cupsogue Deepened Two Feet This Summer — Bunker Found It First
subhead: A building full moon and a reshaped inlet channel are tightening bait schools right where the bass will need to find them.
body_markdown:
The sandbar geometry at Moriches Inlet has been quietly rewriting itself all summer, and it matters more this week than it has in months. The main channel off Cupsogue has scoured a little deeper on the ebb — charter guys running out early are marking an extra foot and a half, maybe two, in the throat where the flood used to shoal up by August. That deeper cut concentrates outgoing current into a tighter lane, and a tighter lane means bait gets funneled instead of spread out over the flats. Bunker schools that would normally scatter across the flood shoal are getting squeezed through that channel on the last of the ebb, which is exactly the kind of structural setup that turns a slow bite into a real one once predators commit.

And predators are starting to commit. The full moon on the 6th and 7th did what building moons do to bait density — it tightened the bunker schools working from Smith Point down through Tuthill Point and out toward the inlet mouth. We flagged this a few days back, saying the moon push into full would concentrate bait further and the first legitimate fall blitz activity was likely within the week. That window is opening now. Reports out of the ocean side off Cupsogue and the inlet's west jetty have blues actively slashing through bunker pods, and stripers are starting to show real interest rather than just picking off the edges the way they were two weeks ago. It's not blitz-level yet inside the bay, but the ingredients are lining up — tighter bait, a building tide, and a channel that's funneling everything through a narrower window of water.

The better bass action this week has been happening on the outside beach, not inside the bay proper. Cupsogue's ocean side, particularly the stretch east of the inlet where the storm-cut sandbar creates a deep trough close to shore, has been giving up slot bass and the occasional overslot on bunker chunks fished on a fish-finder rig, cast just past the second bar into that trough. First light and the last two hours of the outgoing tide have been the window — the current pulls bait out of the inlet and stacks it against that trough edge, and bass are working it before the sun gets high. Bluefish have been mixed in with those bass, mostly in the 3 to 6 pound class, hitting the same chunk baits and also taking well to metal — Kastmasters and diamond jigs worked with a fast retrieve through the wash.

Inside the bay, the pattern is more mixed. Fluke fishing is winding down from its summer peak, which tracks with what's happening across the rest of the South Shore as water starts to ease off its warmest readings and fish begin staging for the fall exit through the inlet. There's still some quality fluke coming from the deeper holes off Tuthill Point and the channel edges near the Route 27 bridge in East Moriches, mostly on bucktail and Gulp combinations — white or pink 3-inch swimming mullets on 3/4-ounce bucktails, dragged slow along bottom on the last of the incoming. But the counts are down from a month ago, and anyone fishing strictly for fluke this week should expect a shorter window and fewer keepers than August delivered.

What hasn't slowed down is the bottom fishing. Porgies remain steady and dependable on the deeper structure inside the bay — the channel drop-offs near Pattersquash and the deeper cuts off Moriches Inlet's inner flats are holding good numbers on standard high-low rigs with clam and squid strips. Blowfish are mixed in with them in the same areas, which is typical for this time of year as both species stage before the water cools further. Blackfish season hasn't opened yet for most of this stretch, but tautog are starting to show around the inlet's rock structure and jetty rubble as a preview of what October will bring once the season does open.

Weakfish have been scarce, which isn't unusual for early September in this system — the better weakfish window here tends to run in the spring and again in a short fall pulse once water temperatures drop into the low 60s. Worth checking again in a few weeks, but it's not a September target right now.

Looking at the next several days, the moon is still working in the fleet's favor. As it eases off full into the coming week, tidal flow stays strong, which should keep bunker schools tight through the inlet and along the ocean beach. The next real trigger to watch is the new moon arriving September 10 — if the bait density keeps building the way it has, that's the tide most likely to produce the first widespread blitz activity inside the bay itself, not just on the outside beach. If there's only one day to fish this week, the smart play is the outgoing tide at first light off Cupsogue, working that trough with bunker chunks and keeping a bucktail rigged for blitz conditions if birds start working. Inside the bay, porgy and blowfish action on the channel edges is the more reliable bet if the ocean side is blown out — check the wind before committing to the beach, since any south or southeast blow will stack chop right into that trough and kill the presentation. Watch the bait. When those bunker schools start balling up tight against the jetty rocks instead of moving through, that's the sign the bass have arrived in numbers worth chasing.
